blocks.text: 1. Objectives, design and data
1.1 Background and objectives

White rust, caused by the oomycete ~~Albugo candida~~, produces white pustules on leaves and stagheads on inflorescences of Indian mustard (~~Brassica juncea~~) and causes large yield losses in India (Saharan et al., 2014). Infected leaves lose pigments and water and change their biochemistry (Mishra et al., 2009), and the disease develops under cool, humid weather (Chattopadhyay et al., 2011). These changes alter canopy reflectance, temperature and texture, which UAV cameras can record (Mahlein, 2016). The methodology follows the disease studies that used the same cameras or the same analysis steps, above all the DT-EDNet study of rice blast (Ma et al., 2026).

blocks.text: 1.5 Rules that hold in every step

items: One sample is one subplot on one date (UAV) or one leaf on one date (ASD). All samples of a plot stay together in the training part or in the test part.
The 15 test plots are fixed before the first flight (Step D1) and are used once, at the end.

Every step that learns from the labels (feature selection for the models, tuning, early stopping, scaling constants) uses the 33 training plots only: GroupKFold(3) by plot for machine learning, 11 of the 33 training plots for the early stopping of the networks.
Objective 1 (description) uses all samples; the same selection steps are repeated on the training plots before any model is built (Step 2.2).
All cameras are measured on the same subplot ROIs; each sample is the field-level average of its ROI (Step B6).
Every sensor model is compared with a covariate-only model, because severity also follows time and weather (Step 2.9).

blocks.text: 2. Part A – Field experiment and data collection

Part A creates every observation used later: the plots and treatments, the UAV images, the leaf scores of 5 plants per subplot and the ASD leaf spectra of the centre plant, the disease index, the covariates, the plant parameters and the independent test data.

blocks.text: Step A1 – Experimental design and treatments

rows: Factorial field experiment at IARI, New Delhi: 4 sowing dates × 3 varieties = 12 treatments, inoculated in three replications (36 plots), plus one uninoculated healthy plot of every treatment in a separate block (12 plots) – 48 plots of 5 m × 3 m.

The design creates a range of severity (different crop ages at inoculation and different varieties) and gives healthy plots of the same age and variety; it also defines the plots that are kept together in the split.

• Mishra et al. (2009): Six Brassica juncea genotypes (including Varuna) inoculated with Albugo candida at 1.44 × 10^{5} zoosporangia mL^{−1}, with uninoculated control plants; disease components and biochemical constituents compared.
• Guo et al. (2021): Wheat yellow rust; inoculated and healthy plots to create a range of disease for UAV hyperspectral detection.
• Liu et al. (2024): Wheat powdery mildew; artificially inoculated and healthy field plots monitored by UAV at early, middle and late infection stages.
• Blasch et al. (2023): Wheat yellow and stem rust; randomised field trial with varieties of different resistance, monitored by UAV and satellite.
• Chattopadhyay et al. (2011): Indian mustard (cv. Varuna and a local cultivar) sown on 10 dates at weekly intervals at Bharatpur, New Delhi and Kangra; white rust related to weather to build forecasting models.

• Mishra et al. (2009): Same host and pathogen; a zoosporangial suspension of similar strength and uninoculated healthy controls.
• Guo et al. (2021): Inoculated replications plus healthy plots create the severity range seen by the UAV.
• Liu et al. (2024): Inoculated and healthy plots create the severity range seen by the UAV.
• Blasch et al. (2023): Three varieties are included so that the models are tested across varieties.
• Chattopadhyay et al. (2011): Staggered sowing dates give crops of different ages under the same weather, for the same crop and disease.

(1) Sow D1 = 19 November, D2 = 26 November, D3 = 3 December and D4 = 10 December 2026 (7-day intervals).
(2) Varieties V1 = PM 26, V2 = Pusa Vijay, V3 = PM 37; plot plan as in the layout figure (healthy 1–12, R3 13–24, R2 25–36, R1 37–48).

(4) Keep the healthy block (plots 1–12) uninoculated, 10 m away from the inoculated block.
(5) Mark each plot with its code (plot number, treatment, replication) and divide it into four quadrant subplots (2.5 m × 1.5 m).

blocks.text: Step A2 – Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) flights and the four cameras

rows: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) flights and the four cameras
On 13 dates the hyperspectral, multispectral, RGB and thermal cameras are flown over the whole field.
Each camera records a different effect of infection: pigments and structure (HS, MS), colour and texture of pustules (RGB), and transpiration (thermal).

• Feng et al. (2022): Wheat powdery mildew; canopy spectra (spectroradiometer), thermal infrared images and RGB images collected in the flowering and filling periods and fused.
• Liu et al. (2024): Wheat powdery mildew; UAV multispectral and thermal images flown between 11:30 and 12:30 h with 80% / 85% overlap at early, middle and late infection stages.
• Calderón et al. (2014): Downy mildew of opium poppy; UAV multispectral and thermal imagery at high resolution.
• Guo et al. (2021): Wheat yellow rust; UAV hyperspectral imaging with reflectance panels.
• Ma et al. (2026): Rice blast; UAV hyperspectral images (400–1000 nm, 1.26 cm ground pixel).
• Nguyen et al. (2023): Spring wheat yellow rust; multispectral UAV imagery: red-edge (690–740 nm) and near-infrared bands separated healthy and severely infected plots.

• Feng et al. (2022): Several sensors measured on the same dates.
• Liu et al. (2024): Multispectral and thermal cameras flown together around midday with high overlap.
• Calderón et al. (2014): UAV thermal + multispectral for a foliar disease.
• Guo et al. (2021): UAV hyperspectral flights with panels.
• Ma et al. (2026): UAV hyperspectral camera at centimetre resolution.
• Nguyen et al. (2023): A multispectral camera with red-edge and near-infrared bands.

(1) Fly between 11:00 and 14:00 h under clear sky and low wind, 30 m above ground, about 85% forward and 80% side overlap.
(2) Place the reflectance panels and the ground control points (GCPs) before every flight; image the panels before and after the flight.
(3) Record air temperature and relative humidity during the flight (needed for thermal conversion, Step B1).
(4) Pre-symptomatic dates: 1, 4 and 7 January 2027 (2, 5 and 8 DAI). Post-symptomatic dates: 11, 18 and 25 January, 1, 8, 15 and 22 February, 1, 8 and 15 March 2027 (12–75 DAI).
(5) On every flight day carry out the leaf scoring and ASD measurements (Steps A3 and A4).
Settings: Hyperspectral: Headwall co-aligned VNIR–SWIR imager, 400–2500 nm (483 usable bands, 399–2398 nm); ground pixel about 2.2 cm.; Multispectral: MicaSense RedEdge-MX, 475, 560, 668, 717, 840 nm; about 2 cm.; RGB: DJI camera, about 0.8 cm. Thermal: FLIR Vue Pro R, 7.5–13.5 µm, 640 × 480 pixels, about 3.9 cm.

blocks.text: Step A3 – Plant scoring and disease index of each subplot

rows: Plant scoring and disease index of each subplot

In every subplot, 5 plants (the centre and the four corners, inside the inner buffer) are tagged; on every flight day their leaves L3, L5 and LL are graded on the 0–9 scale. The 15 grades of a subplot give its disease index (DI).
The DI is the reference (label) of every UAV model; five plants spread over the subplot represent the area seen by the cameras, and the centre plant also carries the ASD readings (Step A4).

• Liu et al. (2024): Wheat powdery mildew; leaves of each plot graded by severity class (national standard) and combined into DI = Σ(grade × leaves)/(highest grade × leaves examined) × 100 as the target of UAV models.
• Mishra et al. (2009): White rust of Indian mustard; DI = sum of all numerical ratings × 100 / (maximum grade × number of leaves examined), on a 0–9 scale (cotyledons) and a 0–5 leaf-area scale (true leaves).
• Conn et al. (1990): Rapeseed and mustard; disease assessment key with drawings of leaves and siliques showing 1, 5, 10, 20, 30 and 50% of the area diseased, stated to be usable also for white rust (Albugo candida).
• Chen et al. (2023): Tobacco viruses; severity scored in grades 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
• Mandal et al. (2023): Rice blast scored on the 0–9 scale and related to leaf spectra.
• Bock et al. (2010): Reviewed visual severity assessment: raters disagree most between neighbouring classes; clear class limits and trained raters reduce error.
• Zhang et al. (2022): Rice leaf blast; the disease grade of each leaf classified from hyperspectral images at the jointing, booting and heading stages.

• Liu et al. (2024): Subplot DI from graded leaves is the target of the UAV models.
• Mishra et al. (2009): Same DI formula for white rust, with grades of leaf area covered by pustules.
• Conn et al. (1990): Area diagrams used to judge the percentage of leaf area with pustules.
• Chen et al. (2023): The same six grade values.
• Mandal et al. (2023): Same 0–9 scale for leaf grades.
• Bock et al. (2010): Written grade limits and one trained scorer for all dates.
• Zhang et al. (2022): Leaf grades recorded on every date across growth stages.

(1) Before inoculation, tag 5 plants in each subplot: the plant nearest the centre and the plants nearest the four corners of the inner buffer (5 × 4 = 20 plants per plot, 960 in the field). The centre plant is the ASD plant.
(2) On each flight day (same day or ± 1 day) grade the 3rd (L3) and 5th (L5) fully expanded leaves from the top and the lowest green leaf (LL) of each tagged plant; count the positions again on every date.
(3) Grade each leaf by the percentage of its area with pustules: 0 = none; 1 = 1–5%; 3 = 6–10%; 5 = 11–25%; 7 = 26–50%; 9 = more than 50%. Judge the percentage with the standard area diagrams of Conn et al. (1990) (leaves with 1, 5, 10, 20, 30 and 50% of the area affected); the same trained person grades all dates.
(4) Subplot DI = Σ(x × f) / (9 × Σf) × 100, where x is the grade and f the number of leaves with grade x (15 leaves per subplot).
(5) From flowering, record staghead severity (%) per subplot = staghead racemes / total racemes × 100.
(6) If a tagged plant dies, tag the nearest healthy-looking neighbour and note the change.
Settings: DI classes (Task B): 0 (DI = 0), 1 (0 < DI ≤ 5), 3 (5 < DI ≤ 10), 5 (10 < DI ≤ 25), 7 (25 < DI ≤ 50), 9 (DI > 50). 2880 leaf grades per date (192 subplots × 15).

Image-based pustule area would avoid rater error but is not available for all leaves in the field; visual grades are the field standard (Bock et al., 2010).

Why five plants? → The centre and four corners spread the scored plants over the subplot seen by the UAV, and 15 leaves give a finer DI than one plant; the leaf-based DI formula is that of Mishra et al. (2009) and Liu et al. (2024).

blocks.text: Step A4 – Leaf spectra with the ASD FieldSpec spectroradiometer on the centre plant of each subplot

rows: Leaf spectra with the ASD FieldSpec spectroradiometer on the centre plant of each subplot

Right after grading, the three graded leaves (L3, L5, LL) of the centre plant of each subplot are measured with the ASD FieldSpec spectroradiometer (contact probe and leaf clip with its own lamp) on all 13 dates.

A leaf spectrum of a graded leaf records the disease without sun, sky, soil or atmosphere and links leaf and canopy data; one plant per subplot keeps the work to one team per date while covering all 192 subplots.

• Mandal et al. (2023): Rice blast; leaf spectra with a handheld spectroradiometer (350–2500 nm) of leaves scored on the 0–9 scale.
• Chen et al. (2023): Tobacco TMV and PVY; leaves measured with an ASD FieldSpec 4 (350–2500 nm) and graded 0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
• Lv et al. (2023): Southern corn leaf blight; leaf-clip spectra (350–2500 nm) for asymptomatic detection and severity classes.
• Selvaprakash et al. (2026): Rice blast (IARI); 800 leaf spectra (350–2500 nm) used for early detection.
• Martínez-Martínez et al. (2018): Bean angular leaf spot; spectra in contact with the leaf estimated severity better than spectra taken above the crop.
• Yu et al. (2021): Pine wilt disease; field portable spectrometer measurements collected with UAV hyperspectral images.
• Mandal et al. (2022): Rice blast (IARI); reflectance of ten genotypes scored 0–9; correlation above 0.6 with severity in 550–760 and 1140–1300 nm.

• Mandal et al. (2023): Leaf spectra of graded leaves, full range.
• Chen et al. (2023): Same instrument class and grade scale.
• Lv et al. (2023): Leaf clip with its own lamp.
• Selvaprakash et al. (2026): A leaf data set of similar size per date is sufficient for leaf models.
• Martínez-Martínez et al. (2018): Contact measurement of single leaves.
• Yu et al. (2021): Leaf spectra collected on the same dates as the UAV flights.
• Mandal et al. (2022): Leaf reflectance of plants scored on the 0–9 scale.

(1) Warm up the instrument; optimise and take a white reference at the start, then every 10–15 minutes or at the start of every plot.
(2) Take 2 readings per leaf on the lamina, avoiding the midrib (each reading = the instrument average of its scans), 350–2500 nm.
(3) Name every file with date, plot, subplot, leaf position and reading number; the leaf grade comes from Step A3.
(4) Measure on the flight day (or ± 1 day); the clip has its own lamp, so the time of day does not matter.
Settings: 576 leaves per date (48 plots × 4 subplots × 1 plant × 3 leaves) × 2 readings = 1152 readings per date; 7488 leaves over 13 dates; about 7 operator-hours per date.

Other ways to reduce the ASD work further: measure only L3 and LL (384 leaves per date); measure on every second post-symptomatic date (8 dates); take 1 reading per leaf. Measuring all 5 plants (2880 leaves per date) is not needed for the leaf models.

Is one plant per subplot enough? → It gives 576 leaves per date, as many per date as the 2025-26 ASD data (419–648 leaves per date), and more than the 800 leaves of a whole rice blast leaf study (Selvaprakash et al., 2026).

blocks.text: Step A5 – Labels and the datasets

rows: Labels of the three tasks are set for every UAV sample (subplot-date) and every leaf; the pre-symptomatic labels are set from the later status.
Each task answers a different question (is it diseased? how severe? what score?) and needs its own models and metrics.

• Lv et al. (2023): Southern corn leaf blight; asymptomatic and symptomatic detection plus severity classes.
• Chen et al. (2023): Tobacco viruses; binary (healthy/infected) and six-grade models.
• Feng et al. (2022): Wheat powdery mildew; classification and regression of severity from fused UAV data.
• Zhu et al. (2017): Tobacco mosaic virus; leaves of inoculated and healthy plants imaged 2, 4 and 6 days after inoculation, before visible symptoms appeared (about 5 days).
• Tian et al. (2021): Rice leaf blast from asymptomatic to mild stages; infected and healthy classes at each stage.

• Lv et al. (2023): Detection task plus severity classes.
• Chen et al. (2023): Task A and six-class Task B.
• Feng et al. (2022): Classification and regression on the same samples.
• Zhu et al. (2017): Separate early-date samples of infected and healthy plants; here infection is confirmed by later symptoms.
• Tian et al. (2021): Separate early-stage labels.

(1) UAV, post-symptomatic dates: Task A = healthy (DI = 0) or diseased (DI > 0), from the survey, not from the treatment; Task B = DI class (0, 1, 3, 5, 7, 9); Task C = DI (%).
(2) If a DI class has fewer than 5% of the samples, merge it with its neighbour (for example 7 + 9) and note it.
(3) ASD leaves (Part L): Task A = grade 0 or > 0; Task B = leaf grade; Task C = leaf grade as a number.
(4) Pre-symptomatic dates (2, 5, 8 DAI): healthy = subplots of the healthy plots; later-infected = inoculated subplots whose DI becomes > 0 on a later date; inoculated subplots that never show pustules are left out.

blocks.text: Step A6 – Covariates and weather

rows: For every sample: DAI, variety, crop age at inoculation, growth stage, 7-day weather and the number of favourable days for white rust.
Severity also follows time, crop stage and weather; these covariates describe the epidemic and form the sensor-free baseline of Steps 2.9, 3.5 and L8.

• Chattopadhyay et al. (2011): White rust of Indian mustard at Bharatpur, New Delhi and Kangra: leaf severity favoured by > 40% afternoon RH, > 97% morning RH and 16–24 °C maximum temperature; staghead by 20–29 °C maximum temperature, aided by > 12 °C minimum temperature and > 97% morning RH; stepwise regression models on weather forecast crop age at first appearance and peak severity.
• Zhang et al. (2014a): Wheat powdery mildew; a logistic regression forecast from meteorological factors alone compared with one that added two remotely sensed features; overall accuracy rose from 69% to 78%.
• Bhattacharya and Chattopadhyay (2013): Mustard rot; surface meteorology combined with satellite remote sensing.
• Blasch et al. (2023): Wheat rusts; detection by UAV changed with the crop growth stage.

• Chattopadhyay et al. (2011): The favourable-day counts use exactly these limits (checked in the full text).
• Zhang et al. (2014a): Weather covariates form the baseline against which the cameras are judged.
• Bhattacharya and Chattopadhyay (2013): Weather combined with sensor data for a mustard disease.

blocks.text: 3. Part B – Unmanned aerial vehicle image processing
Part B turns the raw images of each date into calibrated, co-registered images on one grid and gives one average value per subplot for every band of every camera (field-level average spectra).

blocks.text: Step B1 – Radiometric calibration

Only calibrated values can be compared between dates, plots and cameras.

• Yuan et al. (2025): Rice bacterial blight; a calibrated white panel placed on the ground before and after the flight for radiometric calibration.

(2) RGB: fixed exposure and white balance on all dates; colour indices (ratios) are used, so overall brightness cancels.
(3) Thermal: radiance to temperature with emissivity 0.98 and the air temperature, humidity and height of each flight.

blocks.text: Step B3 – Hyperspectral quality control and smoothing

Water-vapour regions and the detector ends are noisy under sunlight; smoothing is needed before the first derivative (Step C1).

blocks.text: Step B4 – Projection and co-registration

blocks.text: Step B6 – Subplot regions of interest and their average spectra

One region of interest (ROI) is drawn inside each subplot, and the mean of all its pixels is taken for every band of every camera on every date: the field-level average spectrum (and temperature) of the subplot.
The subplot is the unit that carries the DI (Step A3); one average per band and subplot gives one sample per subplot-date, and averaging many pixels reduces noise.

Reflectance of the 483 bands, their first derivative and three red-edge parameters.
The derivative removes brightness offsets and sharpens the red edge; chlorophyll loss moves the red edge to shorter wavelengths.

blocks.text: 5. Part D – Data split and data preparation
Step D1 – The 7:3 split by whole plots

rows: The 48 plots are divided once into 33 training plots and 15 test plots. All samples of a plot – its 4 subplots on all dates and its 12 ASD leaves per date – go to the same side. Healthy and inoculated plots are split separately.

The test plots must be fixed before any step learns from the data; whole plots are kept together because subplots and leaves of one plot share soil, microclimate and inoculum, and a test on new plots is what the model will face.

• Ma et al. (2026): Rice blast; samples divided by stratified sampling into training and test sets at 7:3, with 10% of the training set as validation; features selected and models trained on the 2023 data and tested on an independent 2024 data set.
• Mandal et al. (2023): Rice blast; data divided by stratified sampling into two-thirds calibration and one-third validation; all modelling on the calibration part.
• Cross et al. (2024): Wheat stripe rust progression from hyperspectral reflectance; models checked with 80:20 hold-out splits repeated 100 times.

• Ma et al. (2026): Same 7:3 proportion and stratification; whole plots are assigned instead of single samples, as the cross-year test of Ma et al. kept test data independent.
• Mandal et al. (2023): A stratified hold-out of about one third, with all modelling on the training part.
• Cross et al. (2024): A hold-out test set kept apart from training, as in recent disease spectroscopy.

(1) Test plots per block type = 30% of the plots: 4 of the 12 healthy plots and 11 of the 36 inoculated plots.
(2) Test plots: 1, 4, 5, 8 (healthy; four different sowing dates, all varieties) and 13, 14, 18, 25, 27, 31, 35, 37, 44, 46, 48 (inoculated; 11 different treatments spread over R1–R3, varieties and sowing dates) – the same plots as in the 2025-26 analysis (same plot plan).
(3) All other 33 plots are training plots.
(4) Write the split column (TEST / TRAIN) into every table before any analysis.

blocks.text: Step D2 – Validation inside the training plots

rows: Settings, feature subsets and stopping epochs are chosen inside the 33 training plots: GroupKFold(3) by plot for machine learning (three rounds of 22 fitting and 11 scoring plots) and a fixed set of 11 validation plots (one third) for the networks.
A model must be tuned on data it is not tested on; tuning on the test plots would make the test accuracy optimistic.

blocks.text: 6. Objective 1 – Characterisation of white rust through multimodal unmanned aerial vehicle sensing

Objective 1 describes how each camera sees white rust and selects the features that carry the disease signal. Post-symptomatic description uses all 1920 subplot-dates of each camera with the DI as target (Activities 1.1–1.7); the pre-symptomatic stage uses the 576 subplot-dates with later-infected vs healthy as target (Activity 1.8). For the models (Objectives 2 and 3) the same selection steps are repeated on the 33 training plots only (Step 2.2).

blocks.text: Activity 1.2 – Optimal wavelengths by Shapley additive explanations and competitive adaptive reweighted sampling
Step 1.2.1 – Effective wavelength ranges from normalised difference spectral index and ratio spectral index maps

rows: Effective wavelength ranges from normalised difference spectral index and ratio spectral index maps

For every pair of HS bands, NDSI = (R_{i} − R_{j})/(R_{i} + R_{j}) and RSI = R_{i}/R_{j} are computed and their R² with the DI drawn as maps; bands in pairs with R² > 0.5 for both indices are the effective ranges.
The maps show which band combinations follow the disease and restrict SHAP-CARS to informative regions.

• Ma et al. (2026): Rice blast; R² contour maps of NDSI and RSI with severity (450–1000 nm, reduced sampling); effective ranges were the regions where R² of both indices exceeded 0.5 (455–503, 520–661 and 702–1000 nm).
• Tian et al. (2021): Rice leaf blast; kept the top 5% of features by separability when choosing disease-sensitive features.
• Huang et al. (2014): Winter wheat diseases; optimised two-band indices from exhaustive band combinations.

• Ma et al. (2026): Same maps, indices and 0.5 threshold.
• Tian et al. (2021): Top-5% fall-back if no pair reaches 0.5.
• Huang et al. (2014): Exhaustive two-band search.

(1) Use the 483 HS bands with reduced sampling (every 2nd band).
(2) Compute R² of NDSI and RSI with the DI for every pair; draw the two maps.
(3) Effective ranges = bands taking part in pairs with R² > 0.5 in both maps; if no pair reaches 0.5, use the pairs in the top 5% of R².
Settings: about 29 000 band pairs per index.
☐ Both maps drawn; effective ranges written in nm.
Effective ranges → 1.2.2; best NDSI and RSI pairs → 1.3.1.

blocks.text: Step 1.2.2 – Optimal wavelengths by Shapley additive explanations and competitive adaptive reweighted sampling

rows: Optimal wavelengths by Shapley additive explanations and competitive adaptive reweighted sampling

Candidates are the R and FD bands inside the effective ranges. (1) A random forest predicts the DI and the bands are ranked by mean |SHAP|; the top-ranked bands are kept. (2) Monte Carlo cross-validation chooses the number of PLS components. (3) CARS eliminates redundant bands; the subset with the best cross-validated performance gives the optimal wavelengths (OW).
Hundreds of correlated bands cannot be given directly to a model; SHAP removes uninformative bands, then CARS removes redundant ones.

• Ma et al. (2026): Rice blast; SHAP-CARS – an ensemble model ranked the bands by mean |SHAP|, MCCV chose the PLS components, CARS eliminated redundant variables over many iterations, and the subset was fixed by validation performance; 12 key wavelengths were kept.
• Tian et al. (2021): Rice leaf blast; disease-sensitive bands selected from leaf spectra before model building.

• Ma et al. (2026): The three stages in the same order.
• Tian et al. (2021): Band selection before the models.

(1) Standardise the candidate bands.
(2) Random forest regression of the DI (500 trees); mean |SHAP| per band (TreeSHAP); keep the top 40%.
(3) MCCV (50 random 80/20 divisions by plot) chooses the PLS components (1–15).
(4) CARS: 50 iterations of PLS-weighted, exponentially decreasing band subsets with adaptive reweighted sampling; keep the subset with the lowest GroupKFold(3) RMSE.
(5) Label the bands R_{λ} or FD_{λ}.
Settings: Random forest 500 trees, seed 42; CARS 50 iterations; MCCV 50 divisions.
☐ OW list of about 10–15 bands with wavelength and type.

Step 1.3.1 – Best normalised difference spectral index and ratio spectral index

rows: Best normalised difference spectral index and ratio spectral index
The NDSI and RSI pairs with the highest R² in the maps (bands at least 10 nm apart) are added as indices.
The best two-band indices are simple, data-driven white rust indices.

• Ma et al. (2026): Rice blast; best NDSI and RSI from the band-pair maps.
• Mandal et al. (2023): Rice blast; new indices RBI = R1148/R1301 and NDBI from the best two-band combination.

• Ma et al. (2026): Same indices.
• Mandal et al. (2023): Best two-band combination as a new index.

blocks.text: Step 1.3.2 – White Rust Index

rows: A three-band index WRI = NDSI(λ_{1}, λ_{2}) + w × R_{λ3} is searched.
A third band can correct an effect that a two-band index cannot; the index is specific to white rust and can be carried to cheaper sensors.

• Mahlein et al. (2013): Sugar-beet diseases; spectral disease indices built as a normalised difference of two wavelengths plus or minus a third; selected wavelengths at least 50 nm apart.
• Zheng et al. (2018): Wheat yellow rust; a new three-band index for Sentinel-2.
• Liu et al. (2026): Wheat powdery mildew; a specific vegetation index developed on the ground and used from UAV.

• Mahlein et al. (2013): Same form and 50-nm rule.
• Zheng et al. (2018): Three-band disease index.
• Liu et al. (2026): A disease-specific index for field use.

• Liu et al. (2024): Wheat powdery mildew; red-edge multispectral indices for severity.

blocks.text: Activity 1.5 – Texture selection and the Tri-band Texture Fusion Index
Step 1.5.1 – Minimum redundancy maximum relevance selection of texture features

rows: Minimum redundancy maximum relevance selection of texture features
The 24 PCA texture features are filtered at |r| ≥ 0.95 and ranked by minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR); the top six are kept.
Texture features are many and correlated; mRMR keeps features relevant to the DI and different from each other.

• Ma et al. (2026): Rice blast; mRMR ranked the texture features; the six with the strongest relevance and smallest redundancy were PC2-Mea, PC3-Mea, PC2-Dis, PC2-Con, PC2-Var and PC2-Hom.

blocks.text: Step 1.5.2 – Tri-band Texture Fusion Index

rows: All ordered triplets of TF1–TF6 are combined with three formulas; the triplet with the highest |r| with the DI is the TTFI.
One combination of three texture features can describe roughness, heterogeneity and structure together.

blocks.text: Step 1.6.2 – Variance inflation factor and the disease-specific feature set

blocks.text: 12. Likely questions of the Advisory Committee

blocks.q: Why a 7:3 split by whole plots?
blocks.a: The 7:3 proportion is that of the DT-EDNet study (Ma et al., 2026) and close to the one-third hold-out of Mandal et al. (2023). Whole plots are assigned so that subplots and leaves of one plot are never in both training and test data; the test then measures performance on new plots.

blocks.q: How are the models tuned without the test plots?
blocks.a: Inside the 33 training plots: GroupKFold(3) by plot for the machine-learning models, as Tian et al. (2021) and Lv et al. (2023) used cross-validation for SFFS and the SVM, and one third of the training plots for the early stopping of the networks, as Ma et al. (2026) used a validation set.

blocks.q: Why five scored plants but only one ASD plant per subplot?
blocks.a: Five plants (centre and corners) give a disease index that represents the subplot seen by the UAV, with the leaf-based formula of Mishra et al. (2009) and Liu et al. (2024). The ASD is slow, so only the centre plant is measured: 576 leaves per date, as many per date as the 2025-26 ASD data, and every ASD leaf still has its own grade (Mandal et al., 2023).

blocks.q: Why one feature-selection method per type of feature?
blocks.a: Bands are many and collinear (SHAP-CARS), indices must separate overlapping classes (ReliefF) and texture features are correlated (mRMR); this is the design of Ma et al. (2026).

blocks.q: What is new for white rust?
blocks.a: A White Rust Index in the form of Mahlein et al. (2013); the first comparison of four UAV cameras and their 15 combinations for white rust; leaf and canopy analysed on the same subplots and dates; and a pre-symptomatic test with labels from the later status (Zhu et al., 2017).

blocks.q: Why compare with a covariate-only model?
blocks.a: Severity follows time and weather (Chattopadhyay et al., 2011); Zhang et al. (2014a) showed that remote sensing must be judged against a weather-only model. The cameras are credited only with their gain over it.

blocks.q: Is the dataset large enough for DT-EDNet?
blocks.a: About 880 fitting and 440 validation samples per task is small for a transformer; this is why identical settings, early stopping and strong ML baselines are used, and why the pseudo-image networks are not used for the pre-symptomatic data.

blocks.q: Why are flowers kept in the subplot average spectrum?
blocks.a: Staghead and inflorescence infection belong to the disease; growth stage is recorded and results are reported by stage so that selected features are not flowering effects (Blasch et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024).

blocks.q: How will the results reach farmers' fields and satellites?
blocks.a: The frozen models are tested once at Bharatpur (Ma et al., 2026); the WRI and selected bands can be simulated for satellite bands as done for yellow rust (Zheng et al., 2018) and rice bacterial leaf blight (Das et al., 2015).
